    #115150. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3851 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    According to recent reports, we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    Sources indicate that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    Sources indicate that for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    Recent findings suggest that this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    Recent findings suggest that each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    Sources indicate that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    It has been revealed that A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    In a recent development, this example reveals how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    Sources indicate that each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    Recent findings suggest that the figure below reveals how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    Industry observers note that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below indicates what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which demonstrated that 0.1 worked best).

    We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then highlighted signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    In a recent development, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    In a recent development, the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    In a recent development, we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    According to recent reports, the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    According to recent reports, merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    Recent findings suggest that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each enhancement below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own enhancement. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    In a recent development, "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    It has been revealed that use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    Industry observers note that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    It has been revealed that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets upcoming tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    Recent findings suggest that we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    Sources indicate that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    Recent findings suggest that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    Sources indicate that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Sources indicate that under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    Sources indicate that we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    In a recent development, results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    It has been revealed that we appreciate the feedback from the consumers and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    It has been revealed that does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    Industry observers note that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    According to recent reports, throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    Sources indicate that thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

    Industry observers note that nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.

    What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

    📅 18 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information.
    • It’s like your computer’s hard drive.
    • Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many people and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    According to recent reports, and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

    In a recent development, even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    Blockchain already being adopted by some major-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    It has been revealed that blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Industry observers note that instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Industry observers note that blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a tech giant's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    According to recent reports, blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    Recent findings suggest that yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Sources indicate that coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain tech giant in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    Sources indicate that generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section.

    #115147. Latest Update: Marketplace Avatar Retention: Node.js Signed Object Storage with Deletion Evidence

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1739 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Marketplace Avatar Retention: Node.js Signed Object Storage with Deletion Evidence

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The page fires during a user avatar upload because deletion_eligible_oldest_age has crossed the team's limit.
    • Short answer: let browsers send large files to object storage with narrowly scoped signed URLs, keep retention decisions in the Node.js SaaS database, and delete only from durable evidence that an object is no longer referenced and its recovery deadline has passed.
    • In a recent development, that distinction is the runbook.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The page fires during a user avatar upload because deletion_eligible_oldest_age has crossed the team's limit. A marketplace seller used a signed object storage write, replaced the avatar, and abandoned another large media transfer; the on-call sees three keys and one uncomfortable question: which bytes can be deleted without breaking a live page or a recovery promise?

    Short answer: let browsers send large files to object storage with narrowly scoped signed URLs, keep retention decisions in the Node.js SaaS database, and delete only from durable evidence that an object is no longer referenced and its recovery deadline has passed. Proxy uploads through the application only when the application must inspect or transform every byte before accepting it. The transfer path changes capacity. It does not settle ownership.

    In a recent development, that distinction is the runbook. A direct upload keeps large media off the application's request path, but a completed transfer can outlive the tab that started it. A proxy gives the server one request to authorize and receive, yet couples Node.js request duration and application capacity to file size. Neither design makes deletion safe by itself.

    It has been revealed that at 02:13, the worst dashboard is a count of "old objects." Age is not intent. An old avatar may still be the current avatar; a recent video may already be abandoned; a replaced image may be inside a promised recovery window. The first action is to trace an object key back to an authenticated marketplace owner, a live database reference, and a recorded deletion deadline. If any link is absent, stop automated deletion for that object class and investigate the evidence producer. Then follow one candidate all the way through the system: find the deletion record, confirm its tenant, identify the domain row that last referenced the key, compare the current state with the state captured when cleanup was scheduled, and inspect the deadline that represents the recovery promise. If the seller restored the listing after the job was queued, the live reference wins. If the avatar was replaced twice, only the keys with no current attachment continue. If an abandoned direct upload never gained a domain reference, its separate cleanup deadline governs. This trace is slower than pressing a delete button, but it turns the incident from storage archaeology into a set of falsifiable checks, and those checks tell the team which missing field or transition to instrument next.

    I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The durable lesson is blunt: queue age tells you that work is late, not whether replaying the work is safe. A deletion worker must assume that its message can arrive twice and that the database may have changed since the message was scheduled. It reloads current state before acting.

    Recent findings suggest that the object store cannot infer the marketplace contract from a key and a timestamp. It does not know that a seller restored a listing, that a newly introduced avatar became current, or that a moderation process still holds a file. Object lifecycle management can expire objects and transition storage classes, so it is useful for data whose prefix and age encode a valid policy. It remains a backstop to an application decision, not a substitute for one.

    In a recent development, work backward from what the on-call needs. A useful deletion record contains an opaque object key, tenant ownership, the domain resource that referenced it, the time deletion became eligible, the recovery deadline, and the final outcome. The record is not a copy of the storage inventory. It is evidence for a business transition.

    Recent findings suggest that the earlier signal is a growing gap between deletion eligibility and confirmed deletion. Measure both the age of the oldest eligible record and the number of eligible records that remain unfinished. Age alone pages during low-volume maintenance or one deliberately retained object. Count alone pages after a normal burst even when workers are catching up. Together, and observed across more than one evaluation window, they tell the operator whether a queue is merely busy or no longer advancing.

    According to recent reports, instrument transitions, not just requests. Emit a counter when a file becomes eligible, when a worker claims the record, when current references block deletion, when the object is removed, and when completion is durably recorded. A histogram from eligibility to confirmation exposes slow progress before the oldest-item alert fires. Structured logs should carry an intent or deletion ID, tenant ID, media class, prior state, next state, and a bounded reason code. Don't log a signed URL because it is a temporary capability.

    Sources indicate that the dashboard then answers a short sequence of operational questions: Is fresh work becoming eligible? Are workers claiming it? Are reference checks blocking a particular media class? Are completions keeping pace? The page should link to that sequence, not to a storage console with millions of unrelated keys.

    The threshold is local policy. I'm not sure there is a defensible universal number, because the right delay depends on the stated recovery window, worker schedule, expected upload volume, and the time an operator needs to intervene. Resolve it with a replay of production-shaped records and a written error budget for deletion delay. A concrete invariant is stronger than a fashionable duration: alert before delayed deletion can violate the user-facing retention promise, while leaving enough time for normal scheduling jitter.

    Choose by where byte-level trust must be established. For routine marketplace avatars and large listing media, the least complex capacity model is a control plane in Node.js and a data plane in object storage. The application authenticates the seller, allocates an opaque key, records the expected ownership and media policy, and issues a short-lived signed write. The browser uploads to that exact destination, then asks the application to finalize. Before attaching the object to an avatar or listing, the application checks the storage attributes promised by its own record.

    It has been revealed that do not treat the browser's success callback as proof of durable application state. The tab can close after bytes arrive but before finalization, or retry finalization after a response is lost. Finalization therefore needs an idempotent result: repeating the same valid request returns the already established attachment rather than creating another one. An issued signed URL is authority to attempt one storage operation within its scope; it is not permission to attach an arbitrary key to a different tenant.

    Recent findings suggest that A server proxy is still the cleaner choice when every accepted file must be decoded, scanned, or transformed synchronously before storage, or when the product only accepts small files and the team values a single request boundary over independent data-plane scaling. The catch is operational: slow clients, large request bodies, ingress limits, and application autoscaling become part of the upload system. It is not suitable for the stated marketplace job when large media should avoid the app server.

    Sources indicate that signed direct upload has its own cost. It introduces an interval in which storage and application state may disagree, so the design needs reconciliation and explicit cleanup. Your mileage may vary across runtimes and storage implementations; test the largest permitted file, an interrupted transfer, an expired signature, a repeated finalization, and a deletion racing with restore. A 40 KB avatar on localhost proves almost nothing about the large-media path.

    Industry observers note that delivery is a separate decision. If a download response is meant to display an avatar inline or save an attachment with a filename, Content-Disposition defines those response semantics. It should not be overloaded into the retention model. How a browser presents bytes and when the system may destroy them are different contracts.

    According to recent reports, the deletion worker should consume a stable record ID, not "delete this key" as an unconditional command. On every attempt it reloads the record, confirms that the deadline is in the past, and asks the domain database whether any live attachment still points at the key. If the object became current again, the correct result is a recorded skip, not a delete followed by repair.

    According to recent reports, this Go sketch indicates the guard around a generic storage interface. The Node.js service can own the records and scheduling; the worker contract stays independent of a vendor SDK.

    Sources indicate that the interface makes the critical review question visible: what happens if the process stops after object deletion but before MarkDeleted? The next delivery must be able to repeat the storage deletion and then record completion. That requires idempotent delete semantics in the chosen adapter and a test that exercises this exact boundary. The code also leaves room for the database implementation to serialize a restore against a deletion claim; the precise transaction mechanism belongs to that database, not to the queue message.

    Keep retention classes explicit rather than applying one age rule to everything:.

    Bucket lifecycle rules can enforce expiration for a deliberately isolated class of abandoned data. Align the key layout, lifecycle timing, and application cleanup deadline so two independent mechanisms do not encode conflicting promises. If the business offers a recovery period, a shorter storage expiry makes that promise false; if nothing ever expires, abandoned direct uploads accumulate without a bound.

    Ship the instrumentation before tightening the page. During deployment, compare eligible, claimed, blocked, deleted, and recorded totals, then inspect the oldest records from each state. Exercise a duplicate queue delivery, a restore just before eligibility, an upload that never finalizes, and a worker restart between storage deletion and database completion. The acceptance criterion is not that every job runs once. It is that every valid object reaches one explainable terminal outcome despite retries.

    False positives have a real cost. An alert set below routine queue jitter trains the on-call to ignore age; an alert based only on count fires during healthy bursts; a page for reference-blocked candidates may punish the worker for correctly protecting live media. Use a lower-urgency ticket for accumulating cleanup that remains inside the retention promise, and reserve a page for sustained lack of progress that threatens that promise.

    Industry observers note that the decision rule is compact: direct signed upload for large marketplace media, application-owned evidence for attachment and retention, and guarded idempotent deletion after the deadline. Stick with a proxy when synchronous byte inspection is the actual requirement. Whichever path carries the upload, make the deletion claim provable before allowing automation to act.

    Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model.
    • Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • It has been revealed that we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly latest great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    It has been revealed that we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    Sources indicate that similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    Industry observers note that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    In a recent development, text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

    We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

    You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

    Sources indicate that to set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

    For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

    Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

    According to recent reports, available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

    If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

    The easiest way to run Inkling 2 locally is with the Llama App, available for macOS and Windows. After you have installed it on your computer, select your preferred GGUF quant on the Hub, click the "Use this model" button and select "Llama".

    Follow the docs to integrate your llama server with agents such as Pi, ChatGPT Desktop, and others.

    Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

    SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

    We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

    We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

    MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

    We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

    The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

    Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

    Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

    It has been revealed that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

    Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

    In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

    It has been revealed that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

    In a recent development, we ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

    In a recent development, the photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

    We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

    Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

    We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

    We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

    OpenTelemetry SLO in Dynatrace: availability and latency in DQL

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that your services send their traces over OTLP, but your reliability targets remain numbers on a wiki page.
    • Goal of this tutorial: create two SLOs in Dynatrace from OpenTelemetry spans, one for availability and one for latency, written in DQL, then check their values.
    • If you are still unsure which indicators to measure, first read how to choose SLIs: the practical method.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that your services send their traces over OTLP, but your reliability targets remain numbers on a wiki page. Without an OpenTelemetry SLO wired to that data, nobody knows whether the service keeps its promise, or how much error budget is left before freezing releases.

    Goal of this tutorial: create two SLOs in Dynatrace from OpenTelemetry spans, one for availability and one for latency, written in DQL, then check their values. The content targets Dynatrace SaaS (Grail, Service-Level Objectives app). One section gives the alternative for Dynatrace Managed.

    If you are still unsure which indicators to measure, first read how to choose SLIs: the practical method.

    According to recent reports, both SLIs are « good events / valid events » ratios. This format makes the error budget readable: 0.5% of requests may fail over the window.

    Before writing the SLI, check the available fields:.

    Critical lines: span.kind == "server" keeps only incoming requests, not outgoing calls. span.status_code carries the OpenTelemetry status. If your HTTP spans are not marked as errors on 5xx responses, filter on http.response.status_code >= 500 instead. The exact field names in Grail are described in the Semantic Dictionary documentation: check them before going further.

    Sources indicate that the SLO app expects a time series that returns a percentage. So we turn the spans into series with makeTimeseries:.

    In the Service-Level Objectives app, create an SLO with a custom SLI, paste the query, then set the target to 99.5 and the window to 28 days. The expected shape (result field name, query timeframe handled by the app) may change: compare with a template offered by the app.

    We measure a ratio of fast requests rather than a percentile. A percentile does not add up over 28 days; a ratio does. Target: 95. Create this second SLO the same way.

    An SLO re-evaluates its query regularly. Querying every span of a high-traffic service is expensive in Grail reads. Two leaner options:.

    Example with an extracted metric (name to adapt to your pipeline):.

    See metrics and histograms with OpenPipeline for the extraction.

    Managed has neither Grail nor DQL. Ingested OpenTelemetry spans become service requests there: a classic SLO can then rely on a metric expression, for example (100)*(builtin:service.errors.server.successCount:splitBy())/(builtin:service.requestCount.server:splitBy()), filtered on the service. Check in the documentation for your version that the OpenTelemetry service does expose these metrics.

    In a recent development, with 99.5% over 28 days and 2 million requests in the window, the budget allows 10,000 failed requests. If 4,000 have already failed halfway through the window, 40% of the budget is consumed: the pace is healthy. If 8,000 have failed in one week, the team slows down releases and prioritises reliability. This rule, written in advance and agreed with product, avoids debates during the incident.

    According to recent reports, spans are enough to start. For a high-traffic service, a derived metric is cheaper and faster to evaluate.

    A 28-day window always contains four full weeks: each weekday weighs the same, which makes SLOs comparable from one period to the next.

    In a recent development, an empty SLI signals no traffic in the interval (division by zero). An SLI above 100 signals a badly filtered numerator. Go back to step 1 and compare the counters.

    Two DQL queries are enough to go from OpenTelemetry traces to availability and latency SLOs. Start with one critical service, validate the numbers in a Notebook, then add the burn rate alerts.

    Recommended next step: present these two SLOs at a team review, together with the release freeze rule tied to the error budget. An SLO that product shares and understands is worth more than a perfect SLO that only on-call looks at. Then review the thresholds after a month of real data.

    Keep the Notebook with your exploration queries: it becomes the reference when someone asks why the SLI dropped, and it shortens the next investigation.

    Sources indicate that span.observer is an independent community blog, not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC. Dynatrace is a trademark of Dynatrace LLC. SaaS features evolve quickly: check their availability in your environment and in the official documentation.

    #115143. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    📅 01 Jun 2022 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (757 w)

    Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

    📅 01 Jun 2022 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
    • An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.
    • Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    Industry observers note that performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Recent findings suggest that smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile people by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    "Stop on reply" sounds like one if statement. It is three matching problems.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (474 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You told a salesperson "no thanks." Two days later: "Just circling back." Their tool had your reply in its inbox the whole time.
    • I build the reply side of a prospecting tool, Phantera.
    • Industry observers note that the subject line is useless.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You told a salesperson "no thanks." Two days later: "Just circling back." Their tool had your reply in its inbox the whole time. It just could not tell that the reply was yours.

    I build the reply side of a prospecting tool, Phantera. Here is what "stop the sequence when the prospect replies" turns into once you write it.

    Industry observers note that the subject line is useless. People change it, delete the "Re:", or answer from a phone that rewrites it.

    Recent findings suggest that what survives is in the headers. Every email you send carries a Message-ID. A reply quotes it back in In-Reply-To (RFC 5322, section 3.6.4). So we match in this order:.

    If none matches, the message is not a reply to anything we sent. It is ignored, and we never store or log it. A tool that reads your inbox should forget everything that is not its business.

    According to recent reports, you email, they answer on LinkedIn. If each channel is watched by its own loop, the next email goes out anyway, and now you look like a bot on two channels.

    According to recent reports, the fix is boring and strict: a reply on any channel marks the lead as "do not contact," and every later step checks that flag before sending, whatever its channel. LinkedIn replies are matched to the lead by the sender id we stored when we sent the LinkedIn message.

    Recent findings suggest that one choice I would make again: the classifier that labels a reply (positive, meeting, neutral, negative) can fail. When it does, the sequence stops anyway. A wrong label costs a re-read. A wrong follow-up costs the relationship.

    "I'm out of the office until the 3rd.".

    Count that as an answer and you stop the sequence, then miss the real reply when they are back. Worse in our case: we keep one reply per send, so the out-of-office would take the slot of the real answer.

    So automatic replies are filtered before the model sees them, with keyword rules in French and English. The detail that took a second pass: the subject rule is anchored at the start. Auto-replies prefix the original subject ("Automatic reply: ..."). A human writing "Re: your question about absence management" must not be filtered, and an unanchored regex happily filters them.

    Sources indicate that A brand upcoming email, outside the thread, from another address. A phone call. A reply in person. Nothing links those to your message, and no tool can guess a conversation it never saw. If a vendor promises otherwise, ask how.

    If the second one stops, your tool thinks a holiday is a "no.".

    What is the worst follow-up you have received after saying no?

    I work on Phantera, B2B prospecting that stops the moment a prospect replies.
